lines.text: In nineteen twenty-five, a man sold the Eiffel Tower. He didn't own it. And the buyer never even went to the police.
Other con artists sold a country that didn't exist, fake paintings to the Nazis, and a luxury festival that turned into a disaster camp.
These are seven of the boldest cons in history, counted down from number seven to number one.
And number one is so bold, it sounds made up. But it really happened.
Number seven. New York, twenty thirteen.
A young woman calling herself Anna Delvey shows up in the city's art and party scene. She says she's a rich German heiress.
Her real name was Anna Sorokin. And her fortune only existed on paper.
Her fake bank statements claimed she had sixty million euros sitting in Swiss accounts.
With that story, she applied for a twenty-two million dollar loan to open a private art club in Manhattan.

els.small: for a private members' art club

lines.text: The loan never came through. But one bank did give her a hundred-thousand-dollar overdraft, and she spent it.
She lived in luxury hotels without paying, and a friend ended up covering a sixty-two-thousand-dollar bill from a trip to Marrakesh.

els.txt: ✈️ Marrakesh trip · paid by a friend

lines.text: In twenty nineteen, a jury in New York found her guilty on eight counts. She got four to twelve years in prison.
And then Netflix paid her three hundred twenty thousand dollars for the rights to her story.
The lesson: a confident story can open doors long before anyone checks the facts.

els.small: Confidence opens doors before anyone checks

lines.text: Number six. The Bahamas, twenty seventeen.
Fyre Festival promised a luxury music weekend on a tropical island, with private jets, villas and celebrities.
Famous models posted a glossy promo video, and one celebrity was paid two hundred seventy-five thousand dollars for a single post.
VIP packages with flights and luxury tents cost up to twelve thousand dollars.
But when the guests landed in April twenty seventeen, there were no villas.
Instead, they found disaster relief tents, wet mattresses, and cheese sandwiches in foam boxes.
The festival was called off that very first weekend, and guests scrambled to get off the island.
The founder, Billy McFarland, had raised more than twenty-seven million dollars from over a hundred investors.
In twenty eighteen, he was sentenced to six years in prison, and ordered to forfeit twenty-six million dollars.
The lesson: when a deal is all hype and no details, slow down.

els.small: All hype, no details? Slow down.

lines.text: Number five. Hamburg, Germany, nineteen eighty-three.
Stern, one of Germany's biggest magazines, announced a sensation: sixty volumes of Adolf Hitler's secret diaries.
A Stern reporter had bought them in secret, for nine point three million marks. That's about three point seven million dollars.
A famous British historian vouched for them at first. Then, at the big press conference, he changed his mind.
Forensic tests quickly showed what they really were: modern fakes.
The forger had even messed up the initials on one cover. Instead of A H, it said F H.
They were written by a forger named Konrad Kujau. He and the reporter both went to prison, and several editors lost their jobs.
The lesson: when you badly want something to be true, you stop checking.

els.small: Wanting it to be true is a trap

lines.text: Number four. The Netherlands, nineteen thirty-seven.
A famous art expert announced a sensational find: a lost painting by the Dutch master Vermeer, called The Supper at Emmaus.
It was bought for five hundred twenty thousand guilders, millions in today's money, and given to a museum in Rotterdam.
But it wasn't a Vermeer. It had been painted by a Dutch artist named Han van Meegeren.
During the war, another one of his fakes ended up with Hermann Göring, one of the most powerful Nazis, who traded a hundred and thirty-seven looted paintings for it.
In nineteen forty-five, van Meegeren was arrested for helping the enemy. He was even threatened with the death penalty.
So he confessed: it's not a Vermeer, it's mine. And to prove it, he painted a brand new Vermeer, while court-appointed witnesses watched.
The collaboration charges were dropped. In nineteen forty-seven, he was convicted of forgery and fraud, and sentenced to one year.
He died just weeks later. Experts estimate his fakes had earned him the equivalent of twenty-five to thirty million dollars today.
The lesson: even experts can be fooled, especially by the thing they've always hoped to find.
Number three. London, eighteen twenty-two.
A Scottish soldier named Gregor MacGregor told high society that he was the ruler of a country called Poyais, in Central America.
He described rich farmland, a growing capital city, and settlers getting wealthy. There was even a guidebook.
In London, investors bought two hundred thousand pounds' worth of Poyais government bonds.
And around two hundred and fifty people packed up their lives and sailed across the Atlantic to their new home.
When they arrived, there was no capital and no farms. Poyais simply didn't exist.
Disease spread through the camps. More than half of the settlers died.
Later, MacGregor was put on trial for fraud in France. And he was acquitted.
The lesson: if you can't check something with your own eyes, don't bet everything on it.

els.small: Can't check it? Don't bet everything.

lines.text: Number two. New York, December twenty-oh-eight.
Bernie Madoff was a Wall Street legend, and a former chairman of the Nasdaq stock exchange.
For decades, his clients got smooth, steady returns, year after year, no matter what the market did.
But there were no real trades. Money from new investors was used to pay the old ones. A Ponzi scheme.
In December twenty-oh-eight, he told his sons the business was one big lie. They reported him to the authorities.
Client statements showed almost sixty-five billion dollars, including gains that were completely made up.
He was sentenced to a hundred and fifty years in prison, the maximum, and died there in twenty twenty-one.
A court-appointed trustee has since recovered billions of dollars for the victims.
The lesson: returns that look too smooth to be true usually are.

els.small: Too smooth to be true? It usually is.

lines.text: Number one. Paris, nineteen twenty-five.

spec.chapsub: THE MAN WHO SOLD THE EIFFEL TOWER

lines.text: A con man named Victor Lustig read that the Eiffel Tower was expensive to maintain. And he had an idea.
Posing as a deputy director of France's postal and telegraph ministry, he invited the biggest scrap metal dealers in Paris to a meeting at a luxury hotel.

els.head: MINISTÈRE DES POSTES ET TÉLÉGRAPHES
els.body: Confidential: you are invited to a meeting at the Hôtel de Crillon…

lines.text: His secret: the tower would be torn down, and one lucky dealer could buy its seven thousand tons of metal.
A dealer named André Poisson wanted the deal badly. He paid twenty thousand dollars in cash, plus fifty thousand more to make sure he won.
Then Lustig left Paris with the money. And Poisson was so embarrassed, he never went to the police.
Lustig even came back to Paris to try it again, but fled when he suspected the police had been tipped off.
Years later, in New York, he was caught with fifty-one thousand dollars in fake bills, and sent to Alcatraz.
Every con on this list worked the same way: a story so good, that people didn't want to check it.

els.txt: a story too good to check

lines.text: An heiress, a festival, lost diaries, a lost painting, a whole country, perfect returns, and the Eiffel Tower.
